title: Users, groups, sessions & sudo
about: Accounts and groups, the files /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow and /etc/group, passwords, su and sudo, sessions and terminals, who is logged in, and the startup files of a shell.

questions.title: Who is root
questions.text: Which statement about the account `root` is correct?

options.t: It is the administrator account, always has UID 0, and is not limited by permission checks.
options.why: It is identified by its UID, not its name.

options.t: It is an ordinary user account, whose name happens to be treated in a special way by some of the programs.
It can be recognised by its home directory, which is always `/home/root` on Linux.
It has UID 1, the lowest number that the system hands out to a user account.

questions.title: Why not work as root
questions.text: Why is it discouraged to use the root account for daily work?

options.t: A typing mistake or a malicious program then runs with unlimited power over the whole system.
Because root cannot run graphical programs, so the desktop would not start for it.
options.why: It can, although it is not advisable.

options.t: Because root is slower than an ordinary user, since every command that root runs is checked twice by the kernel.
Because root cannot use the network, which is reserved for ordinary users.

questions.title: Tasks that usually require root
questions.text: Select the operations an ordinary user normally cannot do.

options.t: Configuring network interfaces.
Mounting a disk that is not listed for user mounts in `/etc/fstab`.
Shutting down the machine (on a multi-user system).
Changing the owner of a file to another user with `chown`.
options.why: Only root may give files away.

options.t: Creating files in their own home directory.
Changing their own password.

questions.title: UID ranges
questions.text: On a typical Debian or Ubuntu system, which UIDs do ordinary (human) users get?

options.t: From 1000 upwards; the numbers below 1000 are for root and the system accounts.
options.why: Older Red Hat systems start at 500.

options.t: From 1 upwards, as soon as the administrator creates the first ordinary account.
options.why: Low numbers belong to the system.

options.t: Only UID 0, which every human user shares with root, but with fewer rights.
From 65534 downwards, which is the number of the account called `nobody`.

questions.title: Kind of account
questions.text: Decide the likely kind of each account on a typical Linux system.

items.why: A login account created for a person.
A regular user with a home directory.
Used by services, not for logging in.

questions.title: nologin
questions.text: What does the shell `/usr/sbin/nologin` (or `/bin/false`) in an account's entry achieve?

options.t: The account cannot get an interactive shell; a login attempt is refused with a message.
The account cannot own files, so nothing can be stored under its name.
The account is deleted from the system the next time that it is used in a login attempt, together with its files.
options.why: It exists but cannot log in interactively.

options.t: The account can log in without a password, as no shell asks for one.

questions.text: Match each command with its purpose (Debian-style tools).

pairs.r: Create a new user with home directory and defaults
Remove a user account
Create a new group

questions.title: The -a in usermod
questions.text: What happens if you run `usermod -G devs luke` (without `-a`)?

options.t: `luke`'s supplementary groups are replaced by `devs` alone, so the other groups are lost.
`luke` is added to `devs` and keeps all of their other groups, as it happens with `-a`.
`luke` becomes the owner of the group `devs`, and may add other users to it.
Nothing happens, because the list of groups of a user is read-only.

questions.title: Group membership takes effect
questions.text: You add a user to a new group while they are logged in. When does the user's shell see the new group?

options.t: After logging out and in again (a new login session), because the group list is read at login.
Immediately, in every terminal that the user already has open on the machine.
options.why: Existing processes keep their old groups.

options.t: Only after the next reboot of the machine, when the group files are read again by the system from the disk.
Never: groups cannot be added to a user account that already exists.

questions.title: Files of the account database
questions.text: Match each file with its content.

pairs.r: One line per account: name, UID, GID, comment, home, shell
The hashed passwords and password ageing data
The groups and their members
Who may run which commands with `sudo`

extras.r: The list of people currently logged in
extras.why: That is kept in a runtime database shown by `who`.

questions.title: Fields of passwd
questions.text: How many colon-separated fields does a line of `/etc/passwd` have?

options.why: name, password marker, UID, GID, comment (GECOS), home directory and shell.
That is the number of fields of `/etc/group`.
That is the number of fields of `/etc/shadow`.
No file in the set has five.

questions.title: Fields of a passwd line
questions.text: Put the fields of `/etc/passwd` in their order, from first to last.

items.why: Says that the hash is in `/etc/shadow`.

questions.title: Which field is the shell
questions.text: In `/etc/passwd`, the login shell is field number `{{0}}` and the home directory is field number `{{1}}`.

questions.title: The x in passwd
questions.text: What does the `x` in the second field of a `/etc/passwd` line mean?

options.t: The password is not stored there; the hash is in `/etc/shadow`.
options.why: Older systems kept hashes in `passwd`, which everybody can read.

options.t: The account is disabled, and the user cannot log in until it is unlocked.
options.why: A locked account shows `!` or `*` in shadow.

options.t: The password is empty, so the user can log in by just pressing Enter.
options.why: An empty password would be a blank field.

options.t: The user is an administrator with the right to run any command.
options.why: Administrators are identified by UID 0 or group membership.

questions.title: Why shadow
questions.text: Why were password hashes moved from `/etc/passwd` to `/etc/shadow`?

options.t: `/etc/passwd` must be readable by everyone, so hashes there could be copied and cracked; `/etc/shadow` is root-only.
options.why: Separate data with different secrecy needs.

options.t: To save disk space, because the hashes take a lot of room in the account database.
To make logins faster, since the system reads the smaller `/etc/passwd` first.
Because `/etc/passwd` was too small to hold the long hashes that the modern algorithms produce for each user.

questions.title: Shadow permissions
questions.text: Which permissions does `/etc/shadow` typically have?

options.t: `-rw-r-----`, owned by root with the group `shadow`.
`-rw-r--r--`, so that every program can read the hashes it needs.
`-rwxrwxrwx`, so that the password tools of any user can change it.
`----------`, owned by `nobody`, so that not even root can read it.

questions.title: Hash and lock markers
questions.text: In the password field of `/etc/shadow`, a value beginning with `{{0}}` (or equal to `*`) means the account cannot log in with a password.
questions.note: `passwd -l user` locks an account by putting `!` in front of the hash.

wrong.why: That would just be a character in a (broken) hash.

questions.title: Hash prefixes
questions.text: Match each prefix in a shadow hash with the algorithm it denotes.

pairs.r: MD5 (obsolete)
SHA-256
SHA-512
pairs.why: A long-time default on many distributions.

pairs.r: yescrypt
pairs.why: The newer default on recent Debian and Ubuntu.

extras.why: Hashes never store the password itself.

questions.title: What is a salt
questions.text: What is the purpose of the random "salt" stored inside a password hash?

options.t: It makes two users with the same password get different hashes, and defeats precomputed (rainbow) tables.
options.why: An attacker must attack each hash separately.

options.t: It encrypts the hash with a secret key that only the administrator knows.
It is the user's secret question, which is asked when the password has been forgotten and must be reset.
It lets root recover the original password whenever a user forgets it.

questions.title: Fields of group
questions.text: How is a line of `/etc/group` built?

options.t: `name:password-marker:GID:member1,member2,...`
options.why: Four fields; the last lists the supplementary members.

options.t: `name:UID:GID:home:shell`, like the fields of a user account
`GID:name`, with the members kept in another file
`name:members`, without any numbers or password marker

questions.title: Primary group
questions.text: The user `luke` has primary group GID 1001 in `/etc/passwd`. Is that user listed in the members field of group 1001 in `/etc/group`?

options.t: Not necessarily: the primary group comes from the GID in `passwd`; the member list holds supplementary members.
Yes, always: every user must be listed as a member of their primary group, or the system refuses the account.
No, and the user does not belong to that group at all, since no entry lists them.
options.why: The user is in that group through the GID field of the `passwd` entry.

options.t: Only if that user is root, since the administrator is listed in every group.

questions.title: Display a user's groups
questions.text: Show the groups of the user `luke`: `{{0}} luke`
questions.note: `id luke` adds the numeric ids as well.

wrong.why: It prints only the current user's name.

questions.title: passwd options
questions.text: Match each command with its effect.

pairs.r: Change your own password
pairs.why: Asks for the old one first.

pairs.r: Set the password of another user
Lock the account's password
pairs.why: Login by password is no longer possible.

pairs.r: Unlock the account
Force a password change at the next login

extras.why: Passwords cannot be shown; only hashes are stored.

questions.title: Can root recover a password
questions.text: Root has forgotten what password a user chose. Can root read it?

options.t: No: only a hash is stored, so root can set a new password but cannot recover the old one.
Yes, by looking at the file with `cat /etc/shadow`, where the passwords of every user are kept in the clear.
Yes, by asking for the status of the account with `passwd -s`, which shows it.
Yes, but only if the user belongs to the group `shadow`, which may read it.

questions.title: su variants
questions.text: Match each command with what it does.

pairs.r: Become root (asking root's password), keeping most of your environment
Become root with a full login environment
pairs.why: Loads root's startup files and HOME.

pairs.r: Become `luke`, asking luke's password
Run one command as root and return

extras.r: Log out of the current session

questions.title: su versus su -
questions.text: What is the practical difference between `su` and `su -`?

options.t: `su -` starts a login shell, loading root's environment, `HOME` and `PATH`; plain `su` keeps much of yours.
options.why: Also the working directory becomes root's home.

options.t: `su -` does not ask for a password, while plain `su` always asks for the password of the target user first.
options.why: Both ask, unless you are root.

options.t: `su` is for root only, while `su -` can be used to become any user.
There is no difference: the dash is ignored by the command.

questions.title: What sudo is
questions.text: What does `sudo command` do?

options.t: It runs one command as another user (root by default), after checking `/etc/sudoers`, asking for **your** password.
It opens a permanent root shell that remains open until you explicitly log out of it with the `exit` command.
It changes your user to root until you log out, for all the commands you type.
It asks for the root password, and then runs the command as the administrator.

questions.title: sudo forms
questions.text: Match each command with its effect.

pairs.r: Run one command as root
pairs.why: Then return to your own shell.

pairs.r: Start a root shell, keeping much of your environment
Start a root login shell
Run a command as the user `luke`
List what you are allowed to run with sudo

questions.title: Benefits of sudo
questions.text: Which is an advantage of `sudo` over sharing the root password?

options.t: Each use is logged with the user's name, rights can be limited per command, and no shared secret has to be changed.
`sudo` needs no password at all, which is why it is quicker than logging in as root.
options.why: It normally asks for the user's password.

options.t: `sudo` gives every user full root rights by default, which is convenient on small systems where everybody is trusted.
`sudo` works without any configuration, since every user may use it after installation.

questions.title: Reading sudoers
questions.text: What does the rule `%admin ALL=(ALL) ALL` mean?

options.t: Members of the group `admin` may run any command on any host as any user.
options.why: The `%` marks a group; the first ALL is the host, `(ALL)` the target user, the last ALL the commands.

options.t: The user called `admin` may run any command as root without a password.
options.why: Without `%` it would be a user.

options.t: It is a comment, which `sudo` ignores when it reads the configuration.
Every user of the system may run any command, as members of a group called `admin`.
options.why: The rule names only a group.

questions.title: NOPASSWD rule
questions.text: What does the sudoers line `ana lab01 = PASSWD: /usr/bin/systemctl, NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/uptime` allow?

options.t: User `ana`, on host `lab01`, may run `systemctl` (with their password) and `uptime` (without it) as root.
options.why: Tags apply to the commands that follow them.

options.t: Root may run `systemctl` and `uptime` on the host `lab01`, but only when it has been asked for its password by `sudo`.
options.why: The first word is the user.

options.t: Everyone may run `uptime` on the host `lab01` without a password, and `systemctl` with one.
`ana` may run any command on the machine, without being asked for a password.

questions.title: Editing sudoers
questions.text: Why should you edit the sudoers file with `visudo` instead of a plain editor?

options.t: `visudo` locks the file and checks its syntax before saving, since a broken sudoers can lock everybody out.
Because the file is in a binary format that an ordinary text editor could not write without corrupting it.
Because only the editor `vi` has the permission to write files inside `/etc`.
Because `visudo` changes the owner of the file to the user who has edited it.

questions.title: Who may read sudoers
questions.text: Why is `/etc/sudoers` normally `-r--r-----` owned by root?

options.t: It controls privilege escalation, so ordinary users should neither read nor change it.
Because it is an executable program that the kernel runs as root at each login.
Because it is a log of the commands run with `sudo`, which only root may read.
To make `sudo` faster, since the system then skips the permission check of the file.

questions.title: The setuid helper
questions.text: How can the `passwd` program, run by an ordinary user, modify the root-only file `/etc/shadow`?

options.t: `passwd` has the setuid bit (mode `4755`), so it runs with the privileges of its owner, root.
options.why: It is written carefully to change only the caller's entry.

options.t: Because `/etc/shadow` is world-writable, so every user is allowed to write in it.
Because every user is secretly a member of the group root while running `passwd`.
Because the kernel skips all the permission checks for programs that are named `passwd`.

questions.title: w versus who
questions.text: Which information does `w` show that `who` does not?

options.t: What each logged-in user is running now, plus the idle time and the system load.
The history of the logins that took place before, including the reboots.
The passwords of the users, in the form of their hashes, for auditing purposes.
The list of the failed logins, with the addresses they came from.

questions.title: last
questions.text: Where does `last` get its data?

options.t: From the login records in `/var/log/wtmp`, which keeps past sessions, reboots and logouts.
From `/etc/passwd`, where the date of the last login of each user is stored.
From the current process list, by looking at which shells are running now.
options.why: Past sessions are not processes anymore.

options.t: From the history file of the shell, which records the commands that were typed in each session of the user.

questions.title: Terminal names

pairs.r: A virtual text console
A pseudo-terminal, e.g. a terminal window or an SSH session
The graphical display

pairs.l: An IP address or host in parentheses
pairs.r: Where a remote connection came from

extras.r: The disk the user logged in from

questions.title: The tty command
questions.text: What does the command `tty` print?

options.t: The name of the terminal device connected to standard input, such as `/dev/pts/0`.
options.why: "not a tty" when input is not a terminal.

options.t: The name of the user who runs the command, as `whoami` does, with the host.
The list of all the terminals that are currently in use, as `who` would show.
The speed of the terminal line, in bits per second, and its current settings.

questions.title: Session types
questions.text: Which statement about login sessions is correct?

options.t: Users can log in on a text console, a display manager or remotely with SSH; each makes a session tied to a terminal.
Only one user can be logged in at a time, because the system has a single keyboard.
Remote logins are impossible unless the machine runs a graphical desktop for the user who connects from outside.
Sessions are not recorded anywhere, so the administrator cannot see who logged in.

questions.title: Remote root login
questions.text: Why is it advisable to forbid `root` logins over SSH?

options.t: An attacker only has to guess one well-known user name, and actions are not tied to a person.
options.why: Two barriers instead of one, with accountability.

options.t: Because root has no password, so anyone could connect to the machine as root.
options.why: Root normally has one, or none for direct login.

options.t: Because SSH cannot handle the account with UID 0, and the connection would always fail at once for that user.
Because root logins over the network are much slower than those of other users.

questions.text: Which file on a Debian-based system would you search to see failed SSH login attempts?

options.t: `/var/log/auth.log`
options.why: It records authentication events such as `Failed password for ... from IP`.

options.t: `/etc/ssh/ssh_config`
`/etc/shadow`
`/var/log/dpkg.log`

questions.title: Which startup file

items.why: Read by login shells of all users.

Run when your login shell exits.

questions.title: Login and non-login shells
questions.text: What is a login shell?

options.t: The first shell of a session, started at login (console, SSH, `su -`), which reads the profile files.
Any shell that asks the user for a password before it lets them type commands.
A shell that is run as root, because only the administrator is able to log in to the system from the console.
A shell that runs scripts, which is started by the kernel without any user present.

questions.title: Where to set PATH
questions.text: You want `~/bin` in your `PATH` for every login session. Where do you put `export PATH="$PATH:$HOME/bin"`?

options.t: In `~/.profile` (or `~/.bash_profile`), which a login shell reads once.
In `/etc/passwd`, on the line of your account, after the name of the shell.
options.why: That file is the account database.

options.t: In `~/.bash_history`, where the shell keeps the settings of the last session.
In a file inside `/tmp`, which every new session reads before it starts.

questions.title: Aliases persistently
questions.text: Where does an alias definition usually go so that it is available in every new terminal?

options.t: `~/.bashrc`
options.why: Read by interactive non-login shells; a login shell often sources it from `~/.profile`.

options.t: `~/.bash_logout`
`/etc/shadow`
`/etc/fstab`

questions.title: Reload without logging out
questions.text: You edited `~/.bashrc` and want the changes in the current terminal without opening a new one. Which command does it?

options.t: `source ~/.bashrc`
options.why: It runs the file in the current shell.

options.t: `bash ~/.bashrc`
options.why: That runs it in a child shell, which ends.

options.t: `./.bashrc`
options.why: The file is not executable and would run in a child.

options.t: `exit`

questions.title: The home directory
questions.text: What is the home directory of a user for?

options.t: It is the user's working area at login, holding their files and personal configuration (dot-files).
It holds the programs of the system, which every user needs in order to work.
It is shared among all the users of the machine, so that they can exchange files with each other easily.
It stores the password of the user, in the form of a hash that only root can read.
